title: WHY DID GOD TELL MEN NOT TO HAVE SEX BEFORE HE CAME DOWN ON MOUNT SINAI? THE ANSWER IS DEEPER THAN YOU THINK.
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD TELL MEN NOT TO HAVE SEX BEFORE HE CAME DOWN ON MOUNT SINAI? THE ANSWER IS DEEPER THAN YOU THINK.

One command. Three days of preparation. A mountain trembling beneath the presence of God. And a misunderstood verse that reveals something breathtaking about holiness, intimacy, and why humanity desperately needs Jesus Christ.
There is something unsettling about Exodus 19:15.
Something that can make even a lifelong Christian stop reading, stare at the page, and ask a question they may have been too embarrassed to ask in church.
Why would God tell married men to stay away from their wives just before revealing Himself at Mount Sinai?
Was sex somehow dirty?
Was marital intimacy offensive to God?
Did physical desire make someone unworthy of standing before His presence?
Or was something far greater happening at the foot of that mountain?
Because when you finally understand what God was doing at Sinai, you may never read this passage the same way again.
And somewhere inside this ancient story is a truth that reaches directly into our modern lives.
Into our marriages.
Our private struggles.
Our distractions.
Our hidden compromises.
And those moments when we claim to want God's presence while refusing to surrender the things competing for our attention.
But before we go any further, we need to be careful.
We cannot force a meaning onto Scripture simply because it sounds powerful.
We must allow Scripture to explain Scripture.
And what the Bible actually reveals is more beautiful, more challenging, and more Christ-centered than the misconception that God was somehow condemning sexual intimacy.
The Israelites had just experienced one of the greatest deliverances in human history.
For generations, Egypt had been their prison.
Their backs knew the weight of slavery.
Their hands knew the cruelty of forced labor.
Their children had grown up beneath the shadow of Pharaoh's power.
Then God intervened.
The plagues came.
The Passover happened.
The Red Sea opened.
And a nation that had once cried beneath Egyptian oppression walked into freedom through the mighty hand of God.
But freedom from Egypt was never the end of the story.
God had not merely brought Israel out of slavery. He was bringing Israel into covenant relationship with Himself.
And that is where Mount Sinai enters the picture.
In Exodus 19:4, God reminds His people:
"Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself." (KJV)
Read those final words again.
"Brought you unto myself."
Not merely brought you into a new geographical location.
Not merely rescued you from an abusive political system.
Not merely given you another chance at national survival.
Brought you to Himself.
The God who delivered Israel wanted them to know whose people they were.
And then came the command that raises so many questions.
Moses told the people:
"Be ready against the third day: come not at your wives." — Exodus 19:15 (KJV)
At first glance, that sounds strange.
But the original Hebrew helps us understand what was being commanded.
The phrase translated "come not at your wives" is:
אַל־תִּגְּשׁוּ אֶל־אִשָּׁה
ʾal-tiggəšû ʾel-ʾiššâ
The verb comes from the Hebrew root נגשׁ (nāgaš), meaning to approach or draw near.
The noun אִשָּׁה (ʾiššâ) means woman or wife, depending on context.
Here, the expression is understood as a prohibition against sexual relations during the period of preparation.
The command was not declaring that women were spiritually inferior.
It was not announcing that marriage was unholy.
It was not establishing a permanent requirement that married couples avoid intimacy whenever they wished to worship God.
It was a specific instruction for a specific moment in Israel's covenant history.
And the surrounding verses explain why the people were preparing.
In Exodus 19:10–11, God instructed Moses to consecrate the people, have them wash their garments, and prepare for the third day.
Why?
Because on that day, the LORD would descend upon Mount Sinai before the eyes of the people.
Imagine standing there.
You have seen the sea divide.
You have watched Egypt's power collapse.
You have eaten manna in the wilderness.
You have followed a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.
And now you are being told that the God who performed those wonders is about to descend upon the mountain before you.
Not as an idol carved by human hands.
Not as a powerless figure imagined by religious tradition.
But as the living God.
The Creator.
The Holy One of Israel.
The One whose presence cannot be treated casually.
And suddenly, the preparation begins to make sense.
This was not an ordinary gathering.
This was not another day of wilderness travel.
Israel was about to witness a terrifying and extraordinary revelation of divine holiness.
But there is another detail that we must not overlook.
The Bible does not explicitly say that sexual intimacy was forbidden because sex itself was sinful or dirty.
In fact, Scripture teaches the opposite.
Genesis 1:28 records God's blessing upon human fruitfulness.
Genesis 2:24 describes the union of husband and wife as becoming one flesh.
And Hebrews 13:4 declares:
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled." (KJV)
That matters.
Because God did not create marital intimacy and then suddenly decide it was shameful.
Sexual union within marriage is part of God's good creation.
So why abstain?
The most responsible answer begins with the biblical distinction between ritual purity and moral sin.
In the Old Testament, certain ordinary bodily experiences could produce temporary ritual uncleanness without being sinful.
Leviticus 15:18, for example, describes a man and woman washing after sexual relations and remaining ceremonially unclean until evening.
The passage does not condemn the married couple for having intercourse.
It describes a temporary ritual condition within Israel's system of holiness.
That distinction is crucial.
Something could be ritually incompatible with approaching a holy place at a particular time without being morally evil.
In Exodus 19, Israel was being consecrated for a unique encounter with God.
Washing their garments, observing boundaries around the mountain, and temporarily abstaining from sexual relations were all connected to the seriousness of that preparation.
The command communicated that this approaching revelation demanded extraordinary attention and reverence.
Some interpreters also see a lesson in temporarily setting aside legitimate pleasures for a sacred purpose.
That is a reasonable spiritual application, especially when considered alongside passages such as 1 Corinthians 7:5.
But we must distinguish that application from an explicit explanation of God's motives.
Exodus does not tell us every reason behind the command.
What it clearly tells us is that Israel was being consecrated before the LORD descended.
And that truth alone should make us tremble.
Because the next scene is unlike anything most of us can imagine.
On the third day, thunder began to roll.
Lightning flashed.
A thick cloud covered the mountain.
A trumpet sounded with terrifying intensity.
The people trembled.
Exodus 19:18 says:
"And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly." (KJV)
Picture it.
The ground shaking beneath your feet.
Smoke climbing into the sky.
Fire surrounding the mountain.
A trumpet growing louder and louder.
And somewhere inside that terrifying display, the voice of God.
No one was casually scrolling through a phone.
No one was pretending this was just another religious meeting.
No one was confusing divine holiness with a pleasant emotional experience.
The people were standing before a revelation of the God who made heaven and earth.
And there was a boundary.
A boundary they were forbidden to cross.
God had warned them not to break through toward the mountain.
Even the priests were commanded to consecrate themselves.
Why?
Because holiness is not something fallen humanity can control.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
We live in a generation that often wants the comfort of God's presence without the discomfort of God's correction.
We want His peace.
But not always His authority.
We want His promises.
But sometimes resist His commandments.
We want Him to heal the consequences of our choices while keeping the choices that wounded us in the first place.
We want Jesus close enough to rescue us.
But not always close enough to confront us.
And if we are willing to be honest, some of us know exactly what that struggle feels like.
You can love God and still wrestle with surrender.
You can attend church and still have private battles.
You can post Bible verses while carrying shame nobody sees.
You can sing about holiness while quietly negotiating with temptation.
You can know the language of Christianity without allowing the truth of Christ to transform the hidden places of your life.
But be careful here.
The lesson of Sinai is not that every human desire is sinful.
Nor is it that the solution to spiritual struggle is to despise the body God created.
The deeper question is whether we recognize God's holiness and respond to Him with reverence, trust, and obedience.
There is a difference between receiving God's gifts with gratitude and allowing any gift to become greater in our hearts than the Giver.
Marriage is good.
Rest is good.
Food is good.
Work is good.
Human affection is good.
But even good things can become disordered when we place them above God.
And sometimes the question is not whether something is inherently sinful.
Sometimes the question is whether we are willing to surrender our priorities when God calls us to a particular act of obedience.
Yet the command at Sinai should never be turned into a universal rule that married Christians must abstain from sex before worship, prayer, communion, or encountering God's presence.
The New Testament does not impose such a requirement.
In fact, the apostle Paul offers an important safeguard.
In 1 Corinthians 7:5, he instructs married believers:
"Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again..." (KJV)
Notice what Paul emphasizes.
Mutual consent.
A limited period.
A spiritual purpose.
And a return to marital intimacy.
The Christian marriage is not meant to become a place where one spouse uses spiritual language to pressure, punish, manipulate, or reject the other.
Biblical devotion does not excuse neglect or coercion.
And no one should use Exodus 19:15 to make a husband or wife feel dirty for enjoying the intimacy God designed for marriage.
That would distort the passage rather than honor it.
But there is something even greater happening in this story.
Something that moves us from Sinai to Calvary.
From trembling beneath a mountain to approaching the throne of grace.
From distance to reconciliation.
From the fear of judgment to the hope found in Jesus Christ.
Because the most astonishing thing about Mount Sinai is not simply that the Israelites had to prepare.
It is that even after their preparation, they could not freely ascend the mountain into God's presence.
They could wash their garments.
They could abstain from marital relations.
They could observe the boundaries.
They could stand at the foot of the mountain and listen.
But those outward preparations could not, by themselves, remove the deeper problem of human sin.
The mountain remained holy.
The boundaries remained real.
And the people still needed a mediator.
Moses went up.
The people remained below.
And centuries later, another Mediator would come.
Not merely another prophet carrying God's message.
Not merely another teacher explaining divine commandments.
But Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God who became flesh.
The sinless Savior who entered our broken world.
The One who touched lepers.
Welcomed repentant sinners.
Forgave the guilty.
Confronted hypocrisy.
And gave His life for those who could never save themselves.
Think about that.
At Sinai, the people were warned not to break through the boundary.
At Calvary, Jesus gave Himself so sinners could be reconciled to God.
That does not mean God's holiness became less serious.
It means Christ accomplished what human effort could never accomplish.
Hebrews 10:19–20 speaks of believers having boldness to enter the holiest by the blood of Jesus, through the new and living way He opened for us.
And Hebrews 12 draws a remarkable contrast between Mount Sinai and Mount Zion.
The writer recalls the terrifying mountain associated with fire, darkness, and trembling.
Then he tells believers:
"But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem..." — Hebrews 12:22 (KJV)
And shortly afterward, he identifies Jesus as "the mediator of the new covenant" (Hebrews 12:24).
Do you see the beauty?
Sinai revealed the seriousness of God's holiness.
Jesus reveals the astonishing cost of bringing sinners into fellowship with that holy God.
The cross does not cancel holiness.
The cross shows how seriously God takes both sin and redemption.
And here is something else worth noticing.
At Sinai, the people prepared for the third day.
And the Gospels proclaim that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day.
That connection is emotionally striking, but we must handle it faithfully.
Scripture does not explicitly teach that the three days of preparation at Sinai were a direct prophecy of Christ's resurrection.
We should not manufacture a prophetic claim that the biblical text itself does not establish.
Still, the two events invite us to reflect on the unfolding story of God's revelation and redemption.
At Sinai, the third day brought a terrifying manifestation of divine presence.
At the empty tomb, the third day brought the triumphant announcement that death had been defeated.
At Sinai, Israel stood trembling before the holy mountain.
Through the risen Christ, believers are invited to draw near to God with confidence grounded not in their own purity, but in the finished work of their Savior.
And that is where this ancient story becomes more than a historical question about sexual abstinence.
It becomes a question about the condition of our hearts.
Because some of us have spent years trying to make ourselves acceptable to God.
We promise to change.
We fail.
We promise again.
We hide.
We return to church.
We feel convicted.
We make another promise.
And then we stumble in the very place where we thought we had finally become strong.
Eventually, shame begins whispering something dangerous.
"God must be tired of you."
"You have disappointed Him too many times."
"Real Christians don't struggle like this."
"You might as well stop praying."
But those whispers are not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not tell us that sin is harmless.
It tells us that sin is serious enough that Christ died for it.
And it does not tell us that we must become perfect before coming to Jesus.
It tells us to come to the One who alone can cleanse, forgive, and transform us.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That is not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and return to the Savior who is faithful.
Repentance is not pretending that the struggle never happened.
It is turning toward God with the truth exposed.
It is confessing what we have tried to justify.
It is laying down what has been destroying us.
It is trusting Christ enough to obey Him, even when obedience is costly.
And transformation is not always instantaneous.
Some wounds require time.
Some habits require persistent resistance.
Some marriages need patient rebuilding.
Some believers need wise pastoral care, honest accountability, and practical support.
But the Christian hope is not built upon the strength of our promises.
It rests upon the grace of God working in those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a secret that nobody knows.
Perhaps your marriage looks peaceful in public but feels painfully distant behind closed doors.
Perhaps you are single and tired of hearing teachings that make you feel spiritually incomplete.
Perhaps you are married and have been made to feel guilty for the very intimacy Scripture calls honorable.
Perhaps you have confused religious performance with genuine surrender.
Or perhaps you have been running from God because you think He is waiting to humiliate you.
Look again at Jesus.
Look at the Savior who told the truth about sin while extending mercy to sinners.
Look at the One who refused to excuse evil but willingly carried the judgment our sin deserved.
Look at the risen Lord who calls the weary and burdened to come to Him.
You do not need to invent another ritual to earn His attention.
You need Christ.
You need the forgiveness He offers.
You need the grace that teaches us to deny ungodliness and live differently.
And you need the truth that holiness is not hatred of the human body.
It is belonging to the God who made us and redeemed us.
That is why Exodus 19:15 matters.
Not because sex is shameful.
Not because women were a spiritual obstacle.
Not because God despises physical affection.
And not because abstinence is a magical formula for receiving divine revelation.
It matters because God was teaching His people to approach His covenant revelation with consecration and reverence.
It matters because the surrounding Scriptures help us distinguish ceremonial uncleanness from moral guilt.
It matters because holy things must not be trivialized.
And ultimately, it matters because Sinai points us toward the larger biblical story in which Jesus Christ becomes the perfect Mediator of a better covenant.
The same God who thundered at Sinai has made Himself known through His Son.
And the invitation to come to Christ is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to be forgiven and made new.
Maybe this is the moment you stop measuring your spiritual life by how religious you appear.
Maybe this is the moment you stop confusing conviction with condemnation.
Maybe this is the moment you finally bring that hidden struggle into the light.
And maybe this is the moment you realize that Jesus did not come merely to improve the public version of your life.
He came to redeem the whole person.
The thoughts nobody hears.
The tears nobody sees.
The choices you regret.
The relationships that need healing.
The sins that require repentance.
The heart that desperately needs grace.
That is the story we cannot afford to forget.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
And when He saves, He does not merely cover our shame with a religious appearance.
He calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
If this Scripture has confronted something in your heart, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply leaving a reaction.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to disclose private details publicly. God knows the whole story even when you can only find the strength to speak a few words.
And if you have experienced the healing grace of Christ, share your testimony. Someone who feels trapped in shame may need to hear that repentance, forgiveness, and restoration are possible.
Not because every word written here is beyond examination. Test what you read against Scripture.
If a struggling believer has confused holiness with self-hatred, send it to them.
If you know a friend who has been hiding from God beneath the weight of guilt, consider tagging them with kindness, or reaching out privately if that would be more respectful.
One conversation may lead someone back to Scripture.
And through the faithful witness of ordinary believers, someone may hear the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around a page.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to sell the illusion that spiritual growth can be purchased.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, understand Scripture, and grow as disciples of Jesus Christ.
There is another way to help this ministry continue.
It is voluntary financial support that helps sustain the work of producing biblical teaching, developing discipleship resources, reaching more readers, and continuing the ministry's mission.
Scripture teaches the importance of generosity in supporting Gospel work.
Galatians 6:6 encourages believers who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That last phrase is important.
Not grudgingly. Not of necessity.
Your first responsibility is faithfulness to Christ, including the commitments and responsibilities He has entrusted to you.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation and ways to encourage the mission. They are not substitutes for Scripture, fellowship, prayer, or genuine discipleship.
The purpose is to make Jesus Christ known.
And if you are unable to give financially, you are no less welcome here.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Christ did not shed His blood to create a membership tier between the forgiven and the unforgiven.
He gave Himself to redeem sinners.
So before you leave, return with me one last time to the mountain.
Imagine the smoke.
The fire.
The trembling ground.
The people standing at a distance.
The command to prepare.
The boundaries no ordinary Israelite could cross.
Now turn your eyes toward Calvary.
See the Savior suffering outside Jerusalem.
See the Lamb of God bearing sin.
Hear His cry.
And remember the words recorded in John 19:30:
"It is finished."
Not "Try harder until you become worthy."
Not "Hide your failures until you look holy."
Not "Earn your way into My presence."
"It is finished."
The sacrifice necessary for our redemption was accomplished by Jesus Christ.
And because He rose again, everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can find forgiveness and new life.
So do not leave this story thinking God hates the intimacy He created.
Do not leave believing religious abstinence can make you your own savior.
Do not leave imagining that the holy God of Sinai has stopped caring about holiness.
Leave remembering that the God who is perfectly holy has opened the way of reconciliation through His Son.
And when the weight of your past tells you that you cannot draw near, remember where your confidence truly comes from.
Not your record.
Not your performance.
Not your ability to conceal your weakness.
But Jesus Christ.
The mountain showed us why we could not approach God on our own; the cross revealed how far God was willing to go to bring us home.
